one_liner: Header-only C++17 mode-q tensor-times-vector product built on BLAS gemv/dot; beat Eigen Tensor, TBLIS and usually TCL in 2019.
what_it_does: Computes one contraction, C = A x_q b (a tensor of order p times a vector along mode q), for any order, mode, extents and non-hierarchical storage layout chosen at runtime. It offers three interfaces: an operator form (A (q)* b on its own tlib::ttv::tensor type), a templated ttv() that takes execution, slicing and fusion policy tags, and a C-style ttv() that takes raw pointers plus shape, stride and layout arrays, so it can run on std::vector or any contiguous buffer. It is not a drop-in for Eigen Tensor or TCL: you call its functions, and it covers only tensor-times-vector, not general contractions. A Python wrapper (ttvpy, numpy arrays) is in the repo.
how_it_is_fast: Loops-over-GEMM (LOG): instead of transposing the tensor (the TTGT approach TCL uses), it views contiguous slices or larger subtensors of A in place as matrices and calls the BLAS sgemv/dgemv (or dot) on each, so no copy or extra memory is needed. Loop fusion collapses the outer loops into one, and OpenMP parallelizes across slices or subtensors, with a mode that splits cores between OpenMP threads and BLAS threads; for large tensors it reaches the BLAS gemv's own throughput. Without a BLAS it falls back to its own OpenMP-SIMD gemv loops.
when_to_use: Repeated mode-q tensor-times-vector products (for example in higher-order power methods, tensor decompositions or multilinear PCA) on dense, contiguous tensors of order 2 to 10
Float or double tensors on a multicore x86-64 Linux box where OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS is already linked
You must contract in place on first-order (column-major), last-order or permuted layouts without allocating a transposed copy
You want a small, header-only dependency instead of a full tensor framework, or a numpy-callable TTV via ttvpy
when_not_to_use: General tensor-tensor contractions or tensor-times-matrix: use TCL or TBLIS (the same author's separate bassoy/ttm repo covers tensor-times-matrix)
Strided views or sparse tensors: elements must be stored contiguously
Complex or other non-float/double element types where speed matters: the BLAS path only calls sgemv/dgemv, and other types fall back to the built-in loops

Non-Linux or non-GCC builds: CI runs only g++ on ubuntu-latest, core detection shells out to lscpu, and the two open issues (2023) report link failures and failing MatrixTimesVector tests on macOS/PowerPC
Applications that set their own BLAS or OpenMP thread counts: the parallel paths reset them globally on each call

integration.dependencies: OpenMP headers (matrix_times_vector.h includes <omp.h> unconditionally); optional BLAS: OpenBLAS (-DUSE_OPENBLAS), Intel MKL (-DUSE_MKL, ILP64 in the shipped mkl.mk) or BLIS (-DUSE_BLIS); googletest for the tests; numpy for ttvpy
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (if constexpr, inline variables, nested namespaces); tested with GCC only (paper runs: GCC 7.3; CI: current Ubuntu g++)
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux documented and CI-tested; other platforms not documented (open issue reports test failures on macOS PowerPC)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The parallel policies call openblas_set_num_threads / mkl_set_num_threads / bli_thread_set_num_threads, omp_set_nested(true) and set per-thread BLAS counts, all process-wide settings, so concurrent calls from several threads, or other BLAS users in the same process, can interfere.

gotchas: The README and wiki say to compile with -DUSE_INTELBLAS for MKL, but the headers only test USE_MKL; with -DUSE_INTELBLAS the code silently builds the non-BLAS fallback

The README's policy names (tlib::execution::blas, tlib::slicing::large, tlib::tensor) predate the 2024 move to the tlib::ttv namespace; the code now uses tlib::ttv::execution_policy::par_blas, slicing_policy::subtensor and so on, so README snippets need adapting

The first parallel call runs popen("lscpu ...") to count physical cores (cached in a function-local static); this spawns a shell, fails quietly where lscpu is absent (it then uses std::thread::hardware_concurrency) and may be unwelcome in sandboxed or setuid processes
Validation errors (bad mode, shape, layout or stride, null pointers) throw std::runtime_error, so the low-level interface is not usable with exceptions disabled
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TTV over TCL when the contraction is specifically tensor-times-vector and you cannot afford TCL's transpose (TTGT) buffers; TCL stays the choice for general contractions and was faster than TTV in a few plotted cases. LIBXSMM and Fastor target small dense GEMM, not tensor-times-vector.
verified_claims_summary: Bassoy's ICCS 2019 paper and the README plots compare TTV (OpenBLAS 0.2.20 gemv/dot, OpenMP, GCC 7.3 -Ofast -march=native) against TCL 0.1.1, TBLIS 1.0.0 and sequential Eigen 3.3.90 on a 10-core Core i9-7900X across 324 symmetric and 1296 asymmetric order-2 to 10 shapes: read off the plots, TTV is mostly 2-8x faster than TBLIS, between 0.3x and 35x of TCL (abstract: 6.1x average, 12.6x maximum over TCL) and peaks near 35 Gflop/s in single precision. The large Eigen ratios (up to about 900x) compare 20 parallel threads with single-threaded Eigen, and the comparison harness is not in the repo.
status_note: Maintained by a single author (last commit 2025-11-02 added a combined OpenMP/BLAS policy; 24 stars, no releases); LGPL-3.0 header-only code is easy to vendor but carries LGPL obligations, and the README badge wrongly says GPL.
